overview:
São Tomé and Príncipe is a country of two main volcanic islands and a scattering of rocky islets in the Gulf of Guinea, about 250 kilometers off the coast of Central Africa. It is the second-smallest country in Africa, covering less ground than New York City, and the equator crosses an islet just south of São Tomé island.

About 230,000 people live here, nearly all of them on São Tomé, the larger island; Príncipe, to the northeast, holds only a few thousand. Portuguese is the official language, and most people also speak a creole such as Forro. The capital, São Tomé, is a small port of pastel-colored colonial buildings, and the country is a republic with an elected president and parliament.

Nobody lived on these islands before Portuguese ships arrived in the 1470s. Cocoa plantations later made them one of the world's great chocolate suppliers, and cocoa still ripens in the shade of the rainforest.
landAndNature: Both islands are the tops of volcanoes rising from the deep Atlantic floor, and rainforest covers most of their steep interiors. Pico de São Tomé reaches 2,024 meters, and towers of hardened lava, including the needle-shaped Pico Cão Grande, stand above the trees. Rain falls heavily in the southwest and much more lightly in the drier north. Because the islands were never joined to the mainland, the plants and animals that arrived by wind, wave, or wing evolved on their own: the giant São Tomé begonia, the world's smallest ibis, and several birds found nowhere else. Sea turtles nest on the beaches, whales pass offshore, and no large predators live on land.
peopleAndCulture: Most islanders descend from Africans brought here by force, along with Portuguese settlers and later contract workers from Angola, Mozambique, and Cape Verde. Portuguese is used in school and government, while Forro, Angolar, and Principense creoles are spoken at home. Meals combine Atlantic fish with tropical crops: calulu, a stew of smoked fish with leafy greens and palm oil, breadfruit, and fried or boiled bananas. The tchiloli, a centuries-old masked play performed to drums and flutes, retells a medieval European legend in island style. Village festivals fill with ússua and socopé dancing, soccer is played on every flat patch of ground, and islanders describe their pace of life as leve-leve, gently gently.
history: Portuguese navigators reached these uninhabited islands around 1470 and began settling them within a few years. Sugar plantations were built with the labor of enslaved Africans, making São Tomé one of the first plantation slave colonies in the world and a model later copied across the Americas. Enslaved people revolted repeatedly, and some escaped into the mountains to form free communities. After sugar declined, coffee and then cocoa took over in the 1800s, worked under conditions so harsh that British chocolate makers boycotted the islands around 1909. Forced labor continued until a massacre of workers in 1953 hardened the independence movement. The country became independent from Portugal on July 12, 1975, and has held multiparty elections since 1991.
funFacts: The equator runs through Ilhéu das Rolas, where a stone marker lets visitors stand with one foot in each hemisphere.
São Tomé and Príncipe was the world's leading cocoa producer in the early 1900s, and cocoa still grows in its forests.
Pico Cão Grande is a needle of solidified lava rising roughly 300 meters straight out of the rainforest.
Príncipe island is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, almost entirely forested and home to fewer than 10,000 people.
No one lived on these islands before the 1470s, so every family here arrived by ship within the last 550 years.
